title: Searching, Sorting and Divide and Conquer
description: Binary search, insertion sort, merge sort and quicksort, the Ω(n log n) lower bound, and the divide-and-conquer strategy.
overview: Searching and sorting are the first algorithms every programmer learns, and they teach the most useful design idea in the subject: divide and conquer. Split a problem into smaller pieces of the same kind, solve each recursively, and combine the answers. Binary search discards half of the data at each step and merge sort sorts the halves separately, and each reduces a linear or quadratic cost to a logarithmic or n log n one.

Machine learning leans on these routines constantly. Decision trees sort each feature to find the best split, ROC curves and AUC are computed by sorting the scores, k-nearest-neighbor search and ranking return the top results, and medians and percentiles need order statistics.
objectives: Implement binary search correctly and state its logarithmic cost and the invariant it maintains.
Implement insertion sort, merge sort and quicksort, and analyze their best, worst and expected running times.
Prove that any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons, and describe sorts that beat the bound by not comparing.
Apply divide and conquer to exponentiation and selection.
Identify where sorting and searching appear in machine learning pipelines.

sections.title: Searching and binary search
body: Play the game of guessing a number between 1 and 100. A good player starts with 50. If told "higher", the number must lie in 51 to 100, so the next guess is 75, and so on. Every guess cuts the remaining range in half, so seven guesses are always enough. Binary search is exactly this strategy, applied to a sorted list. Finding a value in an unsorted list requires checking items one by one: O(n). If the list is **sorted**, **binary search** does far better. Compare the target with the middle item: if equal, done; if the target is smaller, search the left half, otherwise the right half. Each comparison halves the range, so at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons are needed: 20 for a million items, 30 for a billion.

code: """Index of target in sorted list xs, or -1."""
lo, hi = 0, len(xs) - 1          # invariant: if target is in xs, it is in xs[lo..hi]
lo = mid + 1               # discard the left half and the middle
hi = mid - 1               # discard the right half and the middle
body.caption: Binary search with its loop invariant. Python's bisect module provides tested versions (bisect_left, bisect_right).

example.title: How many steps?
example.problem: How many comparisons does binary search need, at most, on 1,000,000 sorted items? How would linear search compare?
example.solution: The range shrinks 10⁶ → 5 × 10⁵ → … → 1, which takes about log₂ 10⁶ = 19.9, so at most 20 comparisons. Linear search needs up to 10⁶: 50,000 times more.

body.warn: Binary search is famously easy to get wrong. Common bugs: using lo < hi instead of lo <= hi (missing the last item), not moving past mid (an infinite loop), and in fixed-width integer languages computing (lo + hi)//2 where lo + hi overflows (use lo + (hi − lo)//2). Write the invariant down and check it for the empty and one-item cases.

body.h: Binary search on a monotone predicate

body: The idea works for any yes/no property that is false up to a threshold and true after it: find the smallest x for which it holds. Examples in machine learning: the smallest learning rate (on a log scale) at which training diverges, the decision threshold that reaches 95% recall, the largest batch size that fits in memory, and the debugging tool `git bisect`, which finds the first bad commit in log₂ n tests.

sections.title: Elementary sorting algorithms
body: **Sorting** arranges items in order. Two properties matter besides speed: a sort is **in place** if it uses O(1) extra memory, and **stable** if items with equal keys keep their original relative order. Stability makes multi-key sorting possible: sort by the secondary key first, then stably by the primary key.
**Insertion sort** builds a sorted prefix: take the next item and slide it left past larger items until it is in position, like sorting playing cards in the hand.

code: while j >= 0 and xs[j] > key:   # shift larger items right
body.caption: Insertion sort: in place and stable.

body: Each shift removes one **inversion**, a pair of items that is out of order (i < j with xs[i] > xs[j]). So insertion sort takes Θ(n + I) time, where I is the number of inversions. For [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] the inversions are (5,2), (5,4), (5,1), (5,3), (2,1), (4,1), (4,3), (6,1), (6,3): I = 9, and the algorithm performs exactly 9 shifts. A sorted list has 0 inversions (best case: O(n)); a reversed list has n(n − 1)/2 (worst case: Θ(n²)).

list: **Selection sort** repeatedly selects the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into place: always Θ(n²) comparisons but only n − 1 swaps.
**Bubble sort** swaps adjacent out-of-order items repeatedly. It is easy to describe and slow; it has no practical use.
Quadratic sorts are fine for very small arrays (under about 20 items) and for nearly sorted data. Real libraries use insertion sort for the small pieces of a faster algorithm.

sections.title: Merge sort and quicksort
body: Both of the fast general-purpose sorts use **divide and conquer**: divide the input, solve the parts recursively, combine.

Imagine two sorted piles of cards, face up. To combine them into one sorted pile you only ever need to look at the top card of each pile: take the smaller one, and repeat. That merging step is fast. Merge sort uses it by splitting the deck in half again and again until each pile has one card (which is trivially sorted), then merging back up. Split the list in half, sort each half recursively, and **merge** the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two front items.

code: while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
if left[i] <= right[j]:          # <= keeps equal items in order (stable)
body.caption: Merge sort. Merging two sorted lists of total length n takes n steps.

body: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n) in every case (see Algorithm Analysis). It is stable and its running time does not depend on the input, but it needs O(n) extra memory. It is also the basis of **external sorting** of data on disk and of sorting in parallel and distributed systems (merging sorted runs).

Quicksort works like sorting a class by height: pick one student as the reference, send everyone shorter to the left and everyone taller to the right, and then repeat inside each group. The reference student is already in the right place after one pass. The method is fast when the reference splits the class roughly in half, and slow when the reference is always the shortest or tallest person. Choose a **pivot**, **partition** the items into those smaller than the pivot and those larger, and sort the two parts recursively. No merging is needed.

code: smaller = [x for x in xs if x < pivot]
equal   = [x for x in xs if x == pivot]
larger  = [x for x in xs if x > pivot]
body.caption: A simple (not in-place) quicksort with a random pivot.

body: If the pivot splits the list evenly each time, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n). If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item (for instance the first item of an already sorted list), T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n) = Θ(n²). A **random pivot** makes the bad case extremely unlikely: the expected running time is O(n log n) for every input. In-place versions with good constants make quicksort the fastest sort in practice on arrays, though it is not stable.

Python's built-in sorted and list.sort use **Timsort**, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that exploits runs of already ordered data: O(n log n) in the worst case, O(n) on sorted input, stable.

To find the median (or any percentile), a full sort is more than needed. **Quickselect** partitions around a pivot as in quicksort, but recurses only into the side that contains the k-th item: expected time O(n). The median-of-medians variant guarantees O(n) in the worst case. NumPy's np.median and np.partition use this idea.

sections.title: The Ω(n log n) lower bound and sorting without comparisons
body: Can a comparison-based sort beat n log n? No. A comparison sort can be viewed as a binary **decision tree**: each internal node is one comparison with two outcomes, and each leaf is the permutation that the algorithm outputs. There are n! possible input orderings, and each must reach a different leaf, so the tree has at least n! leaves. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves, so 2^h ≥ n!, and the worst-case number of comparisons is at least

body.eq: h ≥ log₂(n!) ≥ (n/2) log₂(n/2) = Ω(n log n)

body: (the last step because n! ≥ (n/2)^{n/2}, taking only the largest n/2 factors; Stirling's formula gives log₂ n! ≈ n log₂ n − 1.44n). Merge sort and heapsort are therefore optimal among comparison sorts.

example.title: A concrete bound
example.problem: What is the minimum number of comparisons that guarantees sorting 10 items?
example.solution: log₂(10!) = log₂(3,628,800) = 21.8, so at least 22 comparisons are needed in the worst case. A simple quadratic sort uses up to 45.

body.h: Beating the bound by not comparing

body: The bound applies only to algorithms that learn about the order solely through comparisons. If the keys are integers in a known small range, we can do better.

list: **Counting sort** sorts n integers from {0, …, k − 1} by counting how many times each value occurs and writing them out in order: O(n + k) time, with O(k) memory. For labels from a few classes it is far faster than any comparison sort.
**Radix sort** sorts d-digit numbers by applying a stable counting sort to one digit at a time, from the least significant: O(d(n + k)).
**Bucket sort** splits uniformly distributed values into buckets and sorts each: O(n) on average.

code: counts[x] += 1                   # count occurrences of each value
body.caption: Counting sort for small integer keys.

sections.title: Divide and conquer, and sorting in machine learning
body: Divide and conquer often turns repeated work into a logarithmic number of steps. **Exponentiation by squaring** computes xⁿ with O(log n) multiplications by using x^n = (x^{n/2})² for even n and x · x^{n−1} for odd n.

code: return half * half if n % 2 == 0 else half * half * x
body.caption: Fast exponentiation. 3¹³ takes 5 multiplications (13 = 1101 in binary), not 12.

body: The same idea gives fast matrix powers (the n-th Fibonacci number from the 2 × 2 matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]]ⁿ in O(log n) steps), and with a different split Karatsuba's multiplication and Strassen's matrix product (see the recurrences in Algorithm Analysis).

body.h: Where machine learning sorts and searches

list: **Decision trees**: to find the best threshold of a numerical feature, sort its m values once, O(m log m), then sweep through them, updating the class counts in O(1) per step to evaluate every split (see Decision Trees). Tree growing costs O(n m log m) per level.

**Rank-based metrics**: the AUC of a classifier is computed by sorting the scores (see the pair-counting example in Evaluating Models): O(m log m). The ROC curve is a sweep over the sorted scores. Quantiles, medians and the median absolute deviation need order statistics.
**Top-k retrieval**: return the k best of m candidates by a heap in O(m log k) or by quickselect in O(m), instead of sorting all of them.
**Nearest neighbor search** in low dimension is a search in a tree structure (k-d tree), the multidimensional analogue of binary search (see Nearest Neighbors).
**Hyperparameter and threshold search** use binary search on a monotone quantity.
**Sorting by length** (bucketing) groups sequences of similar length into a batch so that little padding is wasted when training on text.

example.title: Counting inversions with merge sort
example.problem: How could you count the number of inversions of an array in O(n log n), instead of O(n²)?
example.solution: Run merge sort. When the merge step takes an item from the right half before the remaining items of the left half, each of those remaining left items forms an inversion with it, so add their number. Summing over all merges counts every inversion once. Kendall's τ rank correlation, which is built on inversions, can therefore be computed in O(n log n).

check.q: To find the best split threshold for a numerical feature, a decision tree algorithm
check.a: sorts the feature values and sweeps through them updating class counts
wrong: uses linear search on the unsorted data for every threshold

quiz.q: What is the worst-case number of comparisons of binary search on 1,000 sorted items?
quiz.why: At most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons are needed, and ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = 9, so 10. Linear search could need all 1,000.

quiz.q: Binary search with lo, hi = 0, len(xs) - 1 and mid = (lo + hi) // 2 looks for 7 in [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]. Which indices does it probe, in order?
quiz.why: mid = 2 holds 5, which is smaller than 7, so lo becomes 3. Then mid = 4 holds 11, which is larger, so hi becomes 3. Finally mid = 3 holds 7.

quiz.q: A programmer changes the loop condition of binary search from lo <= hi to lo < hi. What does it return for xs = [1, 3, 5] and target 5?
quiz.why: The first probe is index 1 (value 3), so lo becomes 2 and lo < hi is false. The loop stops with the one remaining candidate, index 2, never examined.

quiz.q: A predicate fits(b) is true for every batch size b up to an unknown limit and false above it, with b between 1 and 1024. About how many evaluations does binary search on b need to find the limit?
quiz.why: Each evaluation halves the remaining range, and log₂ 1024 = 10. Trying every value from the bottom would take up to 1024 training runs.

quiz.q: How many shifts does insertion sort perform on [4, 1, 3, 2]?
quiz.why: Each shift removes one inversion. The inversions are (4, 1), (4, 3), (4, 2) and (3, 2), so there are 4 shifts. The reversed list would have all 6 pairs.

quiz.q: The records A2, B1, C2, D1 (the digit is the key) are sorted by key with a stable sort. What is the resulting order?
quiz.why: A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order, so B stays before D and A stays before C. The other options each reverse at least one tied pair.

quiz.q: Selection sort runs on a list of 1,000 items. Roughly how many comparisons and how many swaps does it make?
quiz.a: About 500,000 comparisons and at most 999 swaps
quiz.why: Selection sort always compares n(n - 1)/2 = 499,500 pairs, but it swaps once per position, at most n - 1 times. That is why it is chosen when writes are costly.

quiz.q: In the merge step of merge sort, the test left[i] <= right[j] is replaced by left[i] < right[j]. What changes?
quiz.a: Equal items from the right half now come out first, so stability is lost
wrong: The running time becomes quadratic, because ties are now compared twice
The result is no longer sorted when the input has repeated values
The sort now needs no extra memory, since ties are never copied
quiz.why: With < an equal pair takes the right-hand item first, which reverses their original order. The output is still sorted and the cost is still n log n.

quiz.q: The three-way quicksort (smaller, equal, larger lists) is run on a list of n identical numbers. What is its running time?
quiz.why: Every item equals the pivot, so equal holds the whole list and both recursive calls get empty lists and stop at once. One pass over the list is all the work.

quiz.q: A sort must guarantee O(n log n) in the worst case and use O(1) extra memory. Which is the best fit?
quiz.why: Heapsort is n log n in every case and works in place. Merge sort needs O(n) extra memory, and randomized quicksort is only expected n log n.

quiz.q: Why can quickselect find the median in expected O(n) time when quicksort needs n log n to sort?
quiz.a: After partitioning it recurses into only the one side that contains the wanted item
wrong: It uses a better pivot that is always the median
It compares each item with the pivot only once for the whole run
It sorts the data with counting sort first
quiz.why: The work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) in expectation, since one half is discarded each time. Quicksort must sort both sides.

quiz.q: A decision tree that sorts 4 distinct items by comparisons must have how many leaves, and so at least how many comparisons in the worst case?
quiz.why: Each of the 4! = 24 orderings needs its own leaf, and a tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves. Since 2⁴ = 16 < 24 ≤ 32 = 2⁵, the height is at least 5.

quiz.q: Counting sort sorts n integers from {0, …, k - 1} in O(n + k) time. Why does this not contradict the Ω(n log n) bound?
quiz.a: It never compares items; it uses the key values as array indices
wrong: The bound holds only for lists of fewer than k items
It makes up for the missing comparisons by using more memory than n
The decision tree argument holds only for stable sorts
quiz.why: The bound is derived for algorithms that learn about the order only through comparisons. Counting sort uses the numeric value of each key directly, which requires a small known range.

quiz.q: Radix sort handles the digits from least to most significant. Why must the sort used on each digit be stable?
quiz.a: Ties on the current digit must keep the order set by earlier digits
wrong: A stable sort is the only kind that works on single-digit keys
It guarantees that no digit is counted twice during the passes
It lets each pass run in constant time, whatever the number of items
quiz.why: Sorting by a later digit must not undo the earlier work on ties. Stability carries the ordering of lower digits through to the end.

quiz.q: How many multiplications does exponentiation by squaring use to compute x⁶⁴?
quiz.why: x⁶⁴ = (x³²)², and each squaring doubles the exponent: x², x⁴, x⁸, x¹⁶, x³², x⁶⁴. That is 6 multiplications rather than 63.

quiz.q: A merge sort counts inversions while merging the sorted halves [2, 4] and [1, 3]. How many inversions are found in this merge?
quiz.why: Taking 1 before the remaining left items 2 and 4 counts 2 inversions. Taking 3 before the remaining left item 4 counts 1 more, for 3 in all.

quiz.q: Why is a batch of text sequences usually built from sequences of similar length?
quiz.a: Little padding is wasted when all the sequences in the batch are about equally long
wrong: Sorting by length makes the model more accurate
Equal-length sequences can be compared in constant time
Short sequences cannot be processed in a batch with long ones
quiz.why: Sequences in a batch are padded to the longest one. Grouping by length (bucketing) cuts the padding, and so the wasted computation.

summary: Binary search finds an item in a sorted array in O(log n) comparisons (20 for a million items), by halving the range while maintaining an invariant. It also applies to any monotone yes/no predicate.
Insertion sort is Θ(n + inversions): quadratic in the worst case, linear on nearly sorted data. Stable sorts keep equal items in order.

Merge sort is Θ(n log n) always, stable, with O(n) extra memory. Quicksort is expected O(n log n) with a random pivot and Θ(n²) in the worst case. Timsort combines merge and insertion sort. Quickselect finds the k-th item in expected O(n).
Every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons (log₂ n! leaves in the decision tree). Counting and radix sort beat it for small-range integers by not comparing.
Divide and conquer also gives fast exponentiation. Machine learning sorts for tree splits and AUC, uses heaps for top-k, and uses binary search for thresholds.

problems.q: Trace merge sort on [4, 1, 3, 2] and count the merge comparisons.
problems.solution: Split: [4, 1] and [3, 2]; then [4], [1], [3], [2]. Merge [4] and [1] → [1, 4] (1 comparison). Merge [3] and [2] → [2, 3] (1 comparison). Merge [1, 4] and [2, 3]: compare 1 vs 2 → 1; 4 vs 2 → 2; 4 vs 3 → 3; then 4 remains: 3 comparisons. Result [1, 2, 3, 4], with 5 comparisons in all.

problems.q: How many inversions does [4, 3, 2, 1] have, and how many shifts does insertion sort perform on it?
problems.solution: Every pair is out of order: C(4, 2) = 6 inversions. Insertion sort performs one shift per inversion: 6.

problems.q: A sorted array has 2²⁰ − 1 = 1,048,575 items. What is the maximum number of comparisons of binary search?
problems.solution: A search tree over n items has height ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons at most: ⌊log₂(2²⁰ − 1)⌋ + 1 = 19 + 1 = 20.

problems.q: Use fast exponentiation to compute 2¹⁰ and list the multiplications.
problems.solution: power(2, 10): half = power(2, 5); power(2, 5): half = power(2, 2), then half·half·2; power(2, 2): half = power(2, 1) = 2 (from power(2, 0) = 1: 1·1·2), giving 2·2 = 4; then power(2, 5) = 4·4·2 = 32; power(2, 10) = 32·32 = 1024. About log₂ 10 ≈ 4 squarings instead of 9 multiplications.

problems.q: You must sort 10⁷ integer class labels, each between 0 and 9. Which sort is best and what does it cost?
problems.solution: Counting sort with k = 10: O(n + k) = about 10⁷ operations and 10 counters of memory, compared with about 2.3 × 10⁸ for a comparison sort.
